text:
The three days of travel may be read as a kind of suspended sentence, in which nothing outward happens and yet everything of consequence is done. The narrator dwells upon the servants, the wood, the knife, and the fire; and by naming them with such care he names the instruments of the act before the act itself. Obedience and horror are kept together through the whole of the journey, and neither is ever suffered to prevail over the other. Faith in this story has the character of an arrangement, of persons and things set in their places, and owes nothing to feeling.

When the scene is compared with the earlier promise, the difference between them narrows. Isaac is the child of the covenant, the one through whom the nations are to be blessed; the writer of Genesis 22 recalls this, and then turns the promise into a test. Everything in the scene turns upon a single word, _hineni_, "here I am," which Abraham speaks three times. The word means something different each time, and each time it costs him more; in Abraham's mouth the language of presence is also the language of loss. He says it first to God, then to Isaac, and last to the angel.
